sheet-1.description: Sheet 1 of the 1891 Hoboken volume shows the southern Hoboken waterfront on the Hudson River, at the foot of Hudson Place, Newark Street and First Street, with River Street running along the top of the sheet. The sheet is turned on the page, with north to the right, and the river along the bottom. Most of the sheet is taken up by the terminal of the Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad: a long train shed with its depot, waiting room and offices, a covered platform, the ferry house with its bridges, waiting room, boiler room and bell tower over the ferry slips, and the ferry routes to Barclay Street and Christopher Street in New York drawn out into the river. To the left the railroad's numbered piers and freight sheds run out into the river, with tracks fanning across them, a coal trestle, an emigrants' waiting room and a Pullman car office near pier 1. To the right of the ferry the long piers of the Hamburg American Packet Company stand at the foot of Newark Street. On the landward side, between River Street and the terminal, a few blocks hold a post office, the Second National Bank, the Evening News, the Hoboken Land and Improvement Company's office building, a storage building and Dukes House. The pierhead and bulkhead exterior line is drawn across the river. Streets carry their widths and corner elevations. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch; only the River Street corners survive as control, so the piers and yards on the left are placed by extrapolation.
notes: Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad ferry terminal, train shed and piers 1 to 6; the present Hoboken Terminal (1907) replaced these buildings.
Hamburg American Packet Company piers at the foot of Newark Street.
Placed from three junctions along River Street only (helmert): low to medium confidence away from River Street.

Hoboken, 50 ft, north to the right. DL&W ferry terminal, piers 1-6 and Hamburg American piers at River St / Hudson Pl / Newark St / 1st St. Helmert from three River Street junctions: low to medium confidence away from River Street.

sheet-2.description: Sheet 2 of the 1891 Hoboken volume shows the Hudson River waterfront between about Second and Fifth Streets. The sheet is turned on the page, with north to the right, so River Street runs left to right along the top edge and the Hudson River fills the bottom, labelled across the lower margin. Along the north side of River Street stand the shops of the Pennsylvania Railroad lessees and the Camden and Amboy Railroad Company, with a lumber shed, boiler shop, blacksmith shop and machine shop, then the Consolidated Iron Works, a cluster of stores including the Thalia Theatre and a hotel, and, nearer Fourth Street, long rows of Campbell and Company stores marked with letters. Beyond them the ground is taken up by the covered piers: the North German Lloyd Steamship Company and Wilson Steamship Company piers occupy a large yellow-shaded block stepping out into the river, and Campbell and Company's Piers No. 1 and No. 2 project further to the right. Fire hose carts, extinguishers and fire pails are listed on the pier sheds. Fourth Street runs off the top of the sheet beside the open ground of Hudson Square, where the street edges are drawn but no blocks are built; two small boat clubs, the Valencia and the Germania, stand on stilts or a bridge at the water edge. Fifth Street is cut along the right edge. The pier slips are shaded pale blue. The sheet carries printed building numbers along River Street and street widths in feet.
notes: Old 2nd, 3rd and Fourth Streets and River Street survive as 2nd, 3rd and 4th Streets and River Street between about 2nd and 4th; the river-front piers and River Street beyond Fourth Street are gone (Sinatra Drive and the Hudson River Waterfront Walkway).
Placed as a helmert from three River Street junctions along one line: low to medium confidence.
Hoboken, 50 ft. River front and piers, River St from 2nd to Fifth St, Hudson Square. Helmert from three River Street junctions (2nd, 3rd, 4th): low-medium confidence.

sheet-3.description: Sheet 3 of the 1891 Hoboken volume covers the river front between Fifth and Sixth Streets and a little beyond, at the north end of Hudson Square. The sheet is turned with north to the right, River Street running along the top and the Hudson River along the bottom, where the water is labelled. Fifth Street is lettered at the left edge, with its corner rounded where it meets River Street, and Sixth Street crosses the sheet a short way to the right. Beside Fifth Street stand a lumber yard and sheds marked Vanderbilt and Schill, and Campbell's stores are drawn as a row of lettered warehouses further down the sheet, with Campbell's pier and a pier belonging to a steamship company projecting into the river as yellow-shaded strips. A broad diagonal street, River Road, crosses the middle of the sheet from upper left to lower right, with a few small buildings along it; a gate house stands at the Sixth Street side. Most of the area between the streets is open, with only a few dwellings drawn on the River Street blocks. At the right of the sheet the grounds hold the Stevens Mansion, a large irregular building with outbuildings, and a smaller pavilion beside it. A public pier is drawn near the water in the lower middle. Street widths of 50, 70 and 75 feet are printed, and block numbers 234, 235, 257 and 258 appear.
notes: Placed by one junction (Fifth Street and River Street, modern 5th Street and River Terrace) with scale and rotation taken from neighbouring sheets: low confidence.
River Road is not in the modern street data; River Terrace is taken as the modern continuation of River Street.
Hoboken, 50 ft. Piers, River Road and the Stevens grounds near Fifth-Sixth St. Anchored on 5th Street / River Terrace (old River St) with 8.1 px/ft, north 77: low confidence.

sheet-4.description: Sheet 4 of the 1891 Hoboken volume covers the largely open ground east of Hudson Street between about Eighth and Eleventh Streets, running down to the Hudson River, the point of land on which the Stevens family estate stood. The sheet is turned on the page, with north to the right and the river along the bottom. Along the top runs a dashed line lettered as the east house line of River Street produced, the line along which River Street was projected; the buildings just above and below it are also drawn at the foot of sheet 10. The ground is divided only by long property lines into the large blocks 258, 259 and 260. Block 258 holds a large detached dwelling of two and a half storeys set in open grounds, with a smaller house, a stable and sheds near the top of the sheet and scattered outbuildings. Block 259 has a hennery and a few small frame buildings. On the far side of a projecting point, block 260 holds the N.J. Yacht Club house near the top, and a row of boat houses stands on the shore below. The old shoreline curves across the sheet from lower left to upper right and back around a narrow inlet, beside which a long pier or bulkhead runs out toward the river. A few buildings stand at the lower left near the line of sheet 3. The pierhead and bulkhead exterior line is drawn near the bottom of the sheet. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch. No street junction is drawn on it, so it is placed from buildings it shares with sheet 10 and the atlas scale and orientation.
notes: Placed from three points carried from sheet 10 (a stable and a building on the River Street line) with the atlas scale and orientation (anchored): low confidence away from the top edge.
Today this ground is the Stevens Institute of Technology campus around Castle Point and Sinatra Drive; the shoreline was later filled.

Hoboken, 50 ft. Stevens grounds east of Hudson St, 8th-11th St, to the river (blocks 258-260, N.J. Yacht Club, boat houses). No junction: anchored on three points carried from sheet 10 (buildings on the East line of River St produced). Low confidence.

sheet-5.description: Sheet 5 of the 1891 Hoboken volume shows the north end of the river front around Thirteenth and Fourteenth Streets, with north to the right. Hudson Street runs along the top edge, with the Hudson River in the lower part of the sheet, where it is lettered across the bottom margin. The principal buildings are the works of W. and A. Fletcher Company, iron works, drawn in pink with a machine shop, boiler shop, blacksmith and flange shop, engine and boiler rooms, a pattern shop and a stable, and a second group in blue, marked as iron buildings, beside Fourteenth Street. A coal pockets building stands at the foot of Fourteenth Street and a coal house beside it, with a short pier and ferry slip drawn out into the river. A lumber yard is lettered in the middle of the sheet, and an open shed and a small dwelling stand near the Ocean Steamship Company's ground at the left. Most of the sheet is open land or water, with the dock outline and bulkhead line drawn in pale blue. Street widths of 50 and 80 feet are printed, along with the block numbers 240, 241, 242, 261, 262 and 263. Fourteenth Street is lettered with the name in full along the right-hand side of the Fletcher works.
notes: Placed by one junction (Fourteenth Street and Hudson Street) with scale and rotation from neighbouring sheets: low confidence.
The riverfront here has been rebuilt; only Hudson Street and 14th Street survive.
Hoboken, 50 ft. Waterfront 11th-14th St east of Hudson St (iron works, 14th St pier). Anchored on 14th St / Hudson St: low confidence.

sheet-6.description: Sheet 6 of the 1891 Hoboken volume shows the Hudson River waterfront at the north end of Hoboken, east of the centre line of Hudson Street produced, up to the line between Hoboken and Weehawken. The sheet is turned on the page, with north to the right and the river along the bottom. Most of the sheet is water and filled ground divided into the large blocks 264 to 269. Along the upper left a bulkhead with a row of small buildings and sheds runs out from sheet 5, and several dry docks project into the river from it, among them the Tietjen and Lang dry docks, with open sheds and small offices on the bulkhead. At the right, two long coal piers run diagonally out into the river from the Weehawken side, crossed by the dash-dot boundary between Hoboken and Weehawken; a reference on the right margin points to Volume 8, sheet 8, for the Weehawken side. The pierhead and bulkhead exterior line is drawn across the river near the bottom of the sheet. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch. Nothing on it survives as a street junction; it is placed from two points carried from sheet 12, where the Weehawken line crosses the centre line of Hudson Street produced, and the atlas orientation.
notes: Placed from two points carried from sheet 12 along the centre line of Hudson Street produced (helmert): low confidence, above all toward the left and bottom of the sheet.
Tietjen and Lang dry docks; coal piers at the Weehawken line. The shoreline has since been filled and rebuilt.
Hoboken, 50 ft. Dry docks and coal piers north of 14th St to the Weehawken line. No junction: two points carried from sheet 12 along the centre line of Hudson St produced. Low confidence.

sheet-7.description: Sheet 7 of the 1891 Hoboken volume covers the blocks around the Hoboken ferry and the north end of Hudson Place and Newark Street. The sheet is turned with north to the right, so Garden, Bloomfield, Washington, Court, Hudson and River Streets run across it from left to right in long rows and First, Second and Newark Streets run up and down. At the left is the broad yard of the railroad, drawn as a mass of tracks, with Ferry Street running along its edge. The main blocks between Ferry Street and Second Street are dense with narrow brick and frame dwellings and stores, and several larger buildings stand out: the North Hudson County Railway Company's depot and stables on Garden Street, a large block of stores between Washington and Hudson Streets, and the City Hall, lettered on the block between Bloomfield and Washington Streets near First Street. Court is the narrow alley between Washington and Hudson Streets. Hudson Place runs from Hudson Street down to River Street between the blocks marked 222, and the blocks near River Street are numbered 222, 223 and 224. Street widths and elevations at the corners are printed, and the block numbers 186 to 212 appear. The tracks at the left lie outside the mask of this part.
notes: The rail yard at the left (Ferry Street and the tracks) was left out of the mask: its tracks are drawn 15 to 22 m from the modern ones.
Ferry Street is not in the modern street data at this place.
Hoboken, 50 ft. Blocks by the ferry, Ferry St (now Observer Highway) to Second St, Garden to River St; DL&W rail yard (x < 4300) masked out (drawn 15-22 m off the modern tracks).

Not georeferenced on this sheet: DL&W / Erie rail yard at the left edge of the sheet (left of x 4300), masked out of part 1 (no street junction; drawn tracks 15-22 m off the modern lines; needs carried points from sheet 1 or parcel corners (step 6b)).

sheet-8.description: Sheet 8 of the 1891 Hoboken volume covers the blocks of central Hoboken between Second and Fifth Streets, with Garden Street at the top and River Street at the bottom. The sheet is turned with north to the right, so the lettered streets cross it from left to right and the numbered streets run up and down. Four rows of blocks are drawn: Garden to Bloomfield, Bloomfield to Washington, Washington to Hudson, with Court as a narrow alley through the middle, and Hudson to River. The blocks are filled with narrow two to four storey dwellings, brick and frame, with stores and small workshops, bakeries, stables and a hall; block numbers 189 to 191, 201 to 203, 213 to 215 and 225 and 226 are printed. Washington Street is wider than the others. At the lower right Fourth, Fifth and River Streets surround the open space of Hudson Square, lettered in large type, which is drawn blank. A compass arrow stands near Fifth Street. The blocks nearest River Street, between Second and Fourth Streets, hold dwellings and stores in long rows, with a few larger buildings. The scale legend and the publisher's notice are printed at the bottom margin. Street widths and elevations are given at most corners.
notes: 5th Street and Washington Street was rejected as an outlier (about 13 m) in the first run; the street may have shifted beside Hudson Square.
Hoboken, 50 ft. Second to Fifth St, Garden to River St, Hudson Square. 5th St / Washington rejected (13 m).

sheet-9.description: Sheet 9 of the 1891 Hoboken volume covers the blocks of central Hoboken between Fifth Street and Eighth Street, from Garden Street at the top of the sheet to River Street at the bottom. The sheet is turned on the page: the numbered streets run up and down it and north points to the right, so Garden, Bloomfield, Washington, Court and Hudson Streets cross the sheet from left to right in long horizontal rows. Garden Street is cut along the top edge and River Street runs along the bottom. The blocks between Garden and Washington Streets are almost entirely built up with narrow two- to four-storey brick and frame dwellings, most with small rear extensions, numbered to the house; Washington Street, drawn much wider than the other streets, carries a mix of stores and dwellings. Court Street, the narrow service alley between Washington and Hudson Streets, is lined with stables and sheds. Between Hudson and River Streets the block from Fifth to Sixth Street holds the buildings of the Stevens Institute, set back in open ground and a smaller detached building beside them; the next block holds a Presbyterian church and a German club stands on Hudson Street at Sixth. Toward Seventh and Eighth Streets on the River Street side the ground is largely open, with a lumber shed and a few frame sheds, and a set of inclined chutes or trestles crosses the corner near Seventh Street. Street widths, house numbers and elevations at the street corners are printed throughout. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch.
notes: Numbered streets are printed in words on this sheet (Fifth, Sixth, Seventh, Eighth); today 5th to 8th Street.
River Street north of 4th Street is today Sinatra Drive or part of the Stevens campus; no River Street junction here is in the modern network.
Stevens Institute (block 227) between Hudson and River Streets, Fifth to Sixth Street.
Hoboken, 50 ft, north to the right. Pilot. Garden to River St, Fifth to Eighth St (printed in words); Stevens Institute block.

sheet-10.description: Sheet 10 of the 1891 Hoboken volume covers the blocks of central-northern Hoboken between Eighth Street at the left edge and Eleventh Street at the right, from Garden Street at the top of the sheet to Hudson Street, with a strip of undivided lots beyond it as far as the east house line of River Street. The sheet is turned on the page: the numbered streets run up and down it and north points to the right, so Garden, Bloomfield, Washington and Hudson Streets cross it in long horizontal rows. Three rows of blocks are drawn in full: blocks 195, 196 and 197 between Garden and Bloomfield Streets, blocks 207, 208 and 209 between Bloomfield and Washington Streets, and blocks 219, 220 and 221 between Washington and Hudson Streets. Almost every frontage is a continuous row of narrow two- to four-storey brick or frame dwellings with house numbers and street elevations printed along the block faces. Larger buildings are few: a Young Men's Christian Association building in block 207, a Baptist Church at the Ninth Street corner of block 208, St Pauls Church in block 219, a bakery on the south side of Bloomfield Street, and stables and sheds in the rear lots. Block 221, at the Tenth Street end, is mostly open ground with a small group of dwellings and a large house with a stable. Below Hudson Street the sheet shows the unbuilt blocks 237, 238 and 239, divided into lots, with only a few dwellings and sheds along their upper edge and a stable and sheds near the foot, ending at a dashed line marked as the east house line of River Street produced. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch and has a compass rose at the lower right.
notes: Numbered streets are printed in words on this sheet (Eighth to Eleventh); today 8th to 11th Street.
River Street is not drawn on this sheet; a dashed line at the foot is lettered as the east house line of River Street produced.
Blocks 237, 238 and 239 below Hudson Street are lotted but largely unbuilt in 1891.
Hoboken, 50 ft. Eighth to Eleventh St, Garden to Hudson St, and lotted blocks 237-239 to the east house line of River St produced (shared with sheet 4).

sheet-11.description: Sheet 11 of the 1891 Hoboken volume covers the blocks of northern Hoboken between Eleventh Street at the left edge and Fourteenth Street at the right, from Park Avenue at the top of the sheet to Hudson Street at the bottom. The sheet is turned on the page: the numbered streets run up and down it and north points to the right, so Park Avenue, Garden, Bloomfield, Washington and Hudson Streets cross it in long horizontal rows. Twelve blocks are drawn, numbered 243 to 254 in four rows of three. The blocks between Park Avenue and Garden Street (252, 253, 254) and between Garden and Bloomfield Streets (249, 250, 251) are filled with continuous rows of narrow two- to four-storey dwellings on their street fronts, with rear sheds, and block 253 shows a regular line of small rear buildings. Blocks 246, 247 and 248 between Bloomfield and Washington Streets are less densely built; block 247 carries a long row of three-storey houses numbered 1 to 26 under the lettering Elysian Place, and block 248 holds a short run of brick fronts, a stable and a small frame building near Fourteenth Street. Blocks 243, 244 and 245 along Hudson Street are largely open lots: block 244 is blank, block 243 has a row of dwellings along its upper edge, and block 245 contains Engine Company No. 4, a few dwellings and a row of seven narrow frame buildings coloured blue-grey that run along Fourteenth Street. At the right edge a stream or ditch with banks drawn in blue curves in from the margin and runs off the sheet; the area beyond the sheet line belongs to the neighbouring sheet. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch and has a compass rose at the upper right.
notes: Numbered streets are printed in words on this sheet (Eleventh to Fourteenth); today 11th to 14th Street.

Elysian Place is lettered in spaced capitals along the north face of block 247; it appears to name the row of houses numbered 1 to 26 rather than a separate street, and is not a street in the modern network.
The stream at the right edge is not named on this sheet.
Hoboken, 50 ft. Eleventh to Fourteenth St, Park Av to Hudson St; Elysian Place row (block 247).

sheet-12.description: Sheet 12 of the 1891 Hoboken volume covers the north end of Hoboken east of Park Avenue and north of Fourteenth Street, up to the line between Hoboken and Weehawken. The sheet is turned on the page, with north to the right: Fourteenth Street runs down the left edge, where the ends of Garden, Bloomfield, Washington and Hudson Streets are lettered, and Park Avenue runs across the top, with 15th Street meeting it from above. Almost the whole sheet is open ground and water: a winding creek or shore line enters from the top near 15th Street, loops back and runs down to the lower left, and a second shore curves along the upper right toward the Weehawken line, which is drawn as a dash-dot boundary across the right side of the sheet with the name Weehawken lettered beside it. The ground is divided only into the large blocks 126, 255, 268 and 269. A few small frame buildings and sheds stand near Park Avenue and along the creek. At the lower left, on Fourteenth Street at the foot of Hudson Street, a cluster of buildings belongs to the waterfront: a hotel, a blacksmith, a ship chandler and small iron-clad buildings, with a shipyard and a tar boiler just beyond. Along the bottom runs a dashed line lettered as the centre line of Hudson Street produced, shared with sheet 6 below. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch. This low ground was later filled and built over; the modern street grid north of Fourteenth Street covers most of it.
notes: Fourteenth Street is printed in words; today 14th Street.
Placed from five junctions along 14th Street and Park Avenue and a hand-picked 14th Street / Hudson Street (14th Street is cut by the left edge of the sheet).
The modern junctions of 15th Street with Garden, Bloomfield, Washington and Hudson Streets fall in the drawn marsh and are excluded.
Hoboken, 50 ft. Marsh and creek north of 14th St and east of Park Av to the Weehawken line. Junctions along 14th St and Park Av only (L-shaped control).

sheet-13.description: Sheet 13 of the 1891 Hoboken volume covers the west side of the town between Garden Street at the bottom and Grand Street at the top, from the railroad yards in the west to Second Street. The sheet is turned with north to the right, so Grand Street, Clinton Street, Willow Avenue, Park Avenue and Garden Street run across it in long rows and First, Second and Newark Streets run up and down. At the left is the railroad yard, a broad band of tracks and Ferry Street along its edge; both are outside the mask of this part. Two diagonal streets, Newark Avenue and Newark Street, cut across the blocks at the left centre, and the blocks along them are narrow and slanted. East of Newark Street the blocks between First and Second Streets are filled with two to four storey dwellings and stores; a lumber yard and lumber sheds stand on the block between Willow and Park Avenues next to Newark Street, a public school number 5 stands on First Street, and a foundry, a bakery and a livery stable appear in the lower blocks. Block numbers 20 to 22, 32 to 34 and 175 to 177 are printed. Street widths of 50 and 65 feet are marked. The scale bars and publisher's notice are at the bottom margin.
notes: The diagonal street at upper left reads Newark Avenue (medium confidence: the lettering is split across two parts of the street).
The rail yard at the left was left out of the mask: its tracks are drawn 15 to 22 m from the modern ones.
Hoboken, 50 ft. Grand to Garden St, Ferry St to Second St, Newark Avenue diagonal; rail yard (x < 4300) masked out.

Not georeferenced on this sheet: DL&W / Erie rail yard at the left edge of the sheet (left of x 4300), masked out of part 1 (no street junction; drawn tracks 15-22 m off the modern lines; needs carried points from sheet 1 or parcel corners (step 6b)).

sheet-14.description: Sheet 14 of the 1891 Hoboken volume covers the south-western part of the city between Second Street at the left edge and Fifth Street at the right, from Grand Street at the top of the sheet to Garden Street at the bottom. The sheet is turned on the page: the numbered streets run up and down it and north points to the right, so Grand, Clinton, Willow, Park and Garden run across it in horizontal rows. Ten drawn blocks are numbered 42, 43, 52, 53, 62, 63, 165, 166, 178 and 179, with Church Square, a large undivided open block, in the lower right between Fourth and Fifth Streets. The blocks are densely built with narrow dwellings and stores on their street fronts and a mix of workshops, sheds and yards behind. Industrial uses include an iron foundry and a bakery in block 165, a wheelwright and a boiler room, machine shop and engine room beside Clinton Street in block 42, a junk shop, a lime, lath, brick, cement and stone yard, and a fire engine house (Engine Company No. 2) on Park Avenue. St Marys Hospital occupies most of the lower side of block 53 on Willow Avenue, and block 63 at the upper right holds the Church of Our Lady of Grace with its tower, a rectory, a school and St Marys Church, with Willow Avenue along its lower edge. Buildings are coloured for construction and a number of small blue-grey sheds appear in the rear lots. House numbers and street elevations are printed on all frontages. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch and has a compass rose at the top.
notes: Numbered streets are printed in words on this sheet (Second to Fifth); today 2nd to 5th Street.
Church Square is the open block between Fourth and Fifth Streets and Park Avenue and Garden Street, the modern Church Square Park.
Willow Avenue is drawn with a small jog where it crosses Third Street.
Hoboken, 50 ft (smaller scan, 14359 px). Second to Fifth St, Grand to Garden St, Church Square.

sheet-15.description: Sheet 15 of the 1891 Hoboken volume covers the south-western blocks of the city between Fifth Street at the left edge and Eighth Street at the right, from Grand Street at the top of the sheet to Garden Street at the bottom. The sheet is turned on the page: the numbered streets run up and down it and north points to the right, so Grand, Clinton, Willow, Park and Garden run across it in horizontal rows. Twelve blocks are drawn, numbered 71, 79, 152, 157, 158, 159, 167, 168, 169, 180, 181 and 182. The upper right is thinly built: block 152 is almost empty apart from two small sheds, block 159 has a few buildings along Eighth Street, and block 79 is partly laid out in empty lots. Block 158, between Clinton and Willow Avenue, is filled by three double rows of small two-storey houses facing two narrow lanes lettered Willow Court. Block 157 holds the American Lead Pencil Works, with its engine room and kilns, a frame school, the Church of the Holy Innocents and a Norwegian Presbyterian Church. Block 167 contains Hoboken Academy, Public School No. 4, a Turn Halle and rows of houses. Block 181 has the Martha Institute and a German Church at the Sixth Street end, a matrass and trimming factory, and a lumber yard with an open shed. Dwellings and stores line the Garden and Park Avenue frontages, with workshops, stables and a wash house in the rear lots. Buildings are coloured by construction and house numbers and street elevations are printed on the block faces. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch and has a compass rose at the top.
notes: Numbered streets are printed in words on this sheet (Fifth to Eighth); today 5th to 8th Street.
Willow Court, two narrow lanes between Clinton Street and Willow Avenue, is not in the modern street network.
Willow Avenue is drawn with a jog at Sixth Street.
Hoboken, 50 ft. Fifth to Eighth St, Grand to Garden St; Willow Court.

sheet-16.description: Sheet 16 of the 1891 Hoboken volume covers the south-western edge of the built-up city between Eighth Street at the left edge and Eleventh Street at the right, from Grand Street at the top of the sheet to Garden Street at the bottom. The sheet is turned on the page: the numbered streets run up and down it and north points to the right, so Grand, Clinton, Willow, Park and Garden run across it in horizontal rows. Fifteen blocks are drawn, numbered 153 to 155, 160 to 162, 170 to 172 and 183 to 185. The upper two rows are almost empty: blocks 153, 154 and 155 between Grand and Clinton Street hold only a few scattered sheds and a Cricket Club House, and blocks 160, 161 and 162 between Clinton Street and Willow Avenue are built up only along their lower edges, with rows of narrow three-storey dwellings and a block of frame partitions. The lower blocks between Willow Avenue and Garden Street are more fully built with continuous rows of three- and four-storey dwellings on the street fronts and stables and sheds behind. Block 172 includes the Hoboken Camera Club, and block 184, between Ninth and Tenth Streets, contains Public School No. 2 with two covered bridges between its wings. Beyond Garden Street the sheet is blank, with the numbers of neighbouring sheets. House numbers and street elevations are printed on all frontages. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch and has a compass rose at the top.
notes: Numbered streets are printed in words on this sheet (Eighth to Eleventh); today 8th to 11th Street.
Most of the blocks between Grand Street and Willow Avenue were laid out but unbuilt in 1891.
The 11th Street / Willow Avenue junction was not detected on this sheet.
Hoboken, 50 ft. Eighth to Eleventh St, Grand to Garden St.

sheet-17.description: Sheet 17 of the 1891 Hoboken volume covers the north-western blocks of the city between Eleventh Street at the left edge and Fourteenth Street at the right, from Adams Street at the top of the sheet to Park Avenue at the bottom. The sheet is turned on the page: the numbered streets run up and down it and north points to the right, so Adams, Grand, Clinton, Willow and Park run across it in horizontal rows. Twelve blocks are drawn, numbered 109, 110, 114 to 117, 151, 156, 163, 164, 173 and 174. This is an industrial and sparsely built part of the town. Block 151 contains a curling rink, block 109 an opaque cloth shade factory with a benzine storage shed outside it, and block 115 an oil cloth factory. Blocks 110 and 116, which share the Hudson County Gas Light Company's works, hold the company's gasometers, a cupola room, retort house, coal shed and a paint works. Block 163 holds Public School No. 6 and a cornice and skylight works, with a brown stone yard beside it, and block 164 has a brown stone works, Fox Hill Flats, an open shed and a blacksmith. Block 117 has a livery stable and storage and a stone yard. Blocks 173 and 174, along Park Avenue, are blank apart from a few buildings. Most of the remaining ground is divided into long unbuilt lots. Fourteenth Street is drawn about 65 feet wide, narrower than its modern width. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch and has a compass rose at the top.
notes: Numbered streets are printed in words on this sheet (Eleventh to Fourteenth); today 11th to 14th Street.
Fourteenth Street is drawn about 65 feet wide; its modern junctions fit 3 to 5 m off the drawn ones, so it was left out of the georeferencing control.
The Hudson County Gas Light Company works occupy blocks 110 and 116.
Hoboken, 50 ft. Eleventh to Fourteenth St, Adams St to Park Av; gas works. 14th St left out (drawn 65 ft against a ~100 ft modern right-of-way west of Park Av; 2.8-4.8 m residuals).

sheet-18.description: Sheet 18 of the 1891 Hoboken volume covers the north-western corner of the city between Fourteenth Street at the left edge and the Hoboken and Weehawken boundary at the right, from Adams Street at the top of the sheet to Park Avenue at the bottom. The sheet is turned on the page: the numbered streets run up and down it and north points to the right, so Adams, Grand, Clinton, Willow and Park run across it in horizontal rows. Fifteenth, Sixteenth and Seventeenth Streets are lettered between the blocks, with Fourteenth Street along the left edge. Most of the sheet is laid out in blocks (121 to 123, 125, 130 to 134, 138, 140, 141, 144 to 146 and 256) divided into long narrow lots with almost nothing built on them. The few buildings are a veneer seating factory (Joel H. Woodman and Company) in block 131, a row of six four-storey buildings called Willow Flats on Willow Avenue, a laundry and blanket works, a lumber yard, a lumber shed and a hay and feed store at the Fourteenth Street end of block 125, and, at the lower right near Park Avenue, a coal pockets and coal trestle belonging to Niven and Company, a stable, a scale house and a hay and feed store. A band of railroad tracks, lettered with the names of the lines, curves across the right side of the sheet; the Hoboken and Weehawken boundary is a dashed curving line, and below Park Avenue the margin shows water along the bottom edge. Margin notes mark Volume 8, Sheet 7 and Sheet 8 where the adjoining sheets of the next volume begin. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch and has a compass rose at the top.
notes: Numbered streets are printed in words on this sheet (Fourteenth to Seventeenth); today 14th to 16th Street, and no 17th Street junction with these streets is in the modern network.
Fourteenth Street is drawn about 65 feet wide (the same as on sheet 17) and was left out of the georeferencing control; Fifteenth Street is drawn narrower than its modern width.
The dashed line marked Boundary is the Hoboken and Weehawken municipal boundary.
Hoboken, 50 ft. Fourteenth to Seventeenth St, Adams St to Park Av, railroad and Weehawken line; mostly unbuilt. 14th St left out. 9 points: medium confidence.

sheet-19.description: Sheet 19 of the 1891 Hoboken volume covers the west side of the town from Monroe Street at the top to Grand Street at the bottom, and from the railroad along Ferry Street at the left to Second Street at the right. The sheet is turned with north to the right, so Monroe, Madison, Jefferson, Adams and Grand Streets run across it in rows and First and Second Streets run up and down. At the left the railroad of the North Hudson County Railway, drawn as a pair of elevated tracks with platforms, runs down beside Ferry Street, and a diagonal street, Newark Street, cuts across the lower left with a brewery and a wagon painter's shop among the slanted lots beside it. Between Ferry Street and Second Street the blocks are almost fully built with narrow two to four storey dwellings, stores, a school and some stables, with a foundry marked on the block between Adams and Grand Streets next to Second Street, a kindling wood yard and a hay and feed store. Block numbers 16 to 18, 28 to 31 and 139 are printed, and street widths of 50, 65 and 70 feet are marked. A compass arrow stands near the top edge. The scale legend and scale of metres are printed at the bottom margin. The Hoboken and Jersey City boundary and the streets of the Jersey City side lie to the left, outside the mask of this part. Houses are numbered along the streets and elevations are given at the corners.
notes: The part of the sheet west of x 4300 (the Jersey City line, Grove, Henderson and Twentieth Streets and Newark Avenue) is outside the mask.
Newark Street is the diagonal street at the lower left; it is not used for control.
Hoboken, 50 ft. Monroe to Grand St, Ferry St to Second St; Jersey City side (x < 4300) masked out.

sheet-20.description: Sheet 20 of the 1891 Hoboken volume covers the blocks of the west side of the city between Second Street and Fifth Street, from Monroe Street along the top of the sheet to Grand Street along the bottom. The sheet is turned on the page: the numbered streets run up and down it and north points to the right, so the named streets cross it from left to right in long horizontal rows. It is drawn at 50 feet to an inch, and street widths (50 and 65 feet), lot depths and house numbers are printed throughout. Block numbers 38 to 41, 48 to 51 and 58 to 61 are printed in the middle of the blocks. This is the most built-up of the western sheets and the only one of the group with much industry. Between Third and Fourth Streets the blocks hold a silk mill with a boiler house (lettered Butler, Rickards and Balas Freres), an iron works with a machine shop and foundry, and a chemical works (lettered Kitz and Grempier). Along Adams Street are Meadow Engine Company No. 3, a variety theatre with a laundry, Public School No. 3, a mouldings mill, a planing mill, a lumber yard, and the large Coffin and Casket factory (Chappell, Chase, Maxwell Co.) with its dry house and storehouse, and Keuffel and Esser's factory beside Third Street. Macaroni and morocco dressing works stand on the block between Fourth and Fifth Streets, together with an Italian Catholic church, stables, hay and feed stores and a blacksmith's. The rest of the blocks are lined with two to four storey dwellings on narrow lots. A scale bar and the copyright line are drawn in the strip below Grand Street.
notes: Numbered streets are printed in words on this sheet; today they are 2nd to 5th Street.
Meadow Engine Company No. 3, Public School No. 3 and Variety Theatre are on the Adams Street block between Second and Third Streets.
Sheet is at 50 feet to an inch; the first-pass fit measures 8.16 px/ft.
Hoboken, 50 ft. Second to Fifth St, Monroe to Grand St; industrial.

sheet-21.description: Sheet 21 of the 1891 Hoboken volume covers the west-side blocks between Fifth Street and Eighth Street, from Monroe Street at the top of the sheet to Grand Street at the bottom. The sheet is turned on the page: the numbered streets run up and down it and north points to the right, so the named streets cross it from left to right in long horizontal rows. It is drawn at 50 feet to an inch, and street widths (50 and 65 feet), lot depths and house numbers are printed throughout. The blocks are numbered 67, 68, 69 and 70 in the first column, 75 to 78 in the second and 82 to 85 in the third. Almost all of the sheet is laid out in narrow lots with few buildings: the upper two rows of blocks, between Monroe and Jefferson Streets, are empty except for a few small sheds on the Sixth Street side. Building is concentrated in the lower left, in the blocks between Jefferson, Adams and Grand Streets and Fifth and Sixth Streets, where rows of two and three storey dwellings and some outbuildings face the cross streets. The block between Sixth and Seventh Streets on Adams Street has a blacksmith and wheelwright and a stable, and a few dwellings stand on the Eighth Street edge. The blocks between Seventh and Eighth Streets are otherwise empty. A scale bar and the copyright line are printed below Grand Street at the lower right.
notes: Numbered streets are printed in words on this sheet; today they are 5th to 8th Street.
Hoboken, 50 ft. Fifth to Eighth St, Monroe to Grand St; mostly empty lots.

sheet-22.description: Sheet 22 of the 1891 Hoboken volume covers the west-side blocks between Eighth Street and Eleventh Street, from Monroe Street at the top of the sheet to Grand Street at the bottom. The sheet is turned on the page: the numbered streets run up and down it and north points to the right, so the named streets cross it from left to right in long horizontal rows. It is drawn at 50 feet to an inch, and street widths (50 and 65 feet), lot depths and house numbers are printed throughout. The blocks are numbered 88 to 91 along Eighth Street and 94 to 96, 98 to 100 in the next columns, with 149 and 150 in the lower right. The sheet is almost empty of buildings: the blocks are drawn as ruled lots, and the only structures are Reynolds Paper Mill with its engine house on the Jefferson Street block next to Eighth Street, a second part of the paper mill on the Adams to Grand block, and one small outbuilding at the foot of the Ninth to Tenth Street block. The blocks between Adams and Grand Streets east of Ninth Street (149 and 150) are drawn as single unsubdivided parcels, and an oblique line cuts across block 91 and block 96, where lot lines end against a diagonal boundary. A scale bar and the copyright line are printed below Grand Street at the lower right.
notes: Numbered streets are printed in words on this sheet; today they are 8th to 11th Street.
9th Street / Adams Street was detected at the drawn position but rejected by the fit (8.6 m).
Hoboken, 50 ft. Eighth to Eleventh St, Monroe to Grand St; Reynolds paper mill. 9th St / Adams rejected (8.6 m).

sheet-23.description: Sheet 23 of the 1891 Hoboken volume covers the north-western corner of the city between Eleventh Street and Fourteenth Street, from the boundary with West Hoboken at the top to Adams Street at the bottom. The sheet is turned on the page: the numbered streets run up and down it and north points to the right, so the named streets cross it from left to right in long horizontal rows. It is drawn at 50 feet to an inch, and street widths (50 and 65 feet), lot depths and house numbers are printed throughout. Monroe, Madison, Jefferson and Adams Streets cross the sheet from left to right; Eleventh, Twelfth, Thirteenth and Fourteenth Streets run up and down. The blocks are numbered 101 to 113. The top of the sheet is crossed by the double and triple tracks of the N. Y. L. E. and W. R. R. and the N. J. J. R. R., which run diagonally from upper left to lower right with the boundary line between Hoboken and West Hoboken drawn as a dash-dot line just below them. Block 106 has a coal pockets and coal trestle along its Monroe Street end, with a stable beside Thirteenth Street, and block 102 has a few dwellings on the Madison Street side. Hillside Road is drawn as an outline above the railroad tracks at the upper right. The rest of the sheet is ruled but unbuilt lots. Neighbouring sheets are marked 28, 22, 24 and 17, and the margin note Vol. 8 Sh. 1 refers to the West Hoboken volume. A scale bar and the copyright line are printed at the lower right.
notes: Numbered streets are printed in words on this sheet; today they are 11th to 14th Street.
Modern 13th and 14th Streets in OpenStreetMap lie several metres from the drawn 13th and 14th Streets; they are not used as control (see georeferencing notes).
Hillside Road is not in the modern street network.
Hoboken, 50 ft. Eleventh to Fourteenth St, Monroe to Adams St, railroad and West Hoboken line at top. 13th and 14th St left out (displaced); placed from 11th and 12th St: medium confidence.

sheet-24.description: Sheet 24 of the 1891 Hoboken volume covers the north-western corner of the city between Fourteenth Street and Seventeenth Street, from the railroad and the West Hoboken boundary at the top to Adams Street at the bottom. The sheet is turned on the page: the numbered streets run up and down it and north points to the right, so the named streets cross it from left to right in long horizontal rows. It is drawn at 50 feet to an inch, and street widths (50 and 65 feet), lot depths and house numbers are printed throughout. Madison, Jefferson and Adams Streets cross the sheet from left to right and Fourteenth, Fifteenth, Sixteenth and Seventeenth Streets run up and down. The blocks are numbered 118 to 120, 127 to 129, 136, 137, 142 and 143. A broad bundle of tracks of the N. Y. L. E. and W. R. R. and the N. J. J. R. R. sweeps across the upper part of the sheet and curves south through the Seventeenth Street block, cutting through the lots of blocks 136, 137 and 143. A dash-dot line marked as the boundary between Hoboken and West Hoboken follows the north edge of the built blocks. Only a few small buildings are drawn, on block 136 beside Sixteenth Street; all other lots are empty. The area north of the boundary is lettered West Hoboken and is blank except for the neighbouring-volume references Vol. 8 Sh. 1, Vol. 8 Sh. 4 and Vol. 8 Sh. 7. A scale bar and the copyright line are printed below the lower right blocks.
notes: Numbered streets are printed in words on this sheet; today they are 14th to 17th Street.
Modern 14th Street in OpenStreetMap lies about 10 m from the drawn street (two ways side by side) and is not used as control.
Hoboken, 50 ft. Fourteenth to Seventeenth St, Madison to Adams St, railroad curve. 14th St left out; hand picks at 16th / Adams and 16th / Jefferson; scale 1.6 percent low: medium-low confidence.

sheet-25.description: Sheet 25 of the 1891 Hoboken volume covers the northwest side of the town from Marshall Street at the upper blocks to Monroe Street at the bottom, between the Jersey City line at the left and Second Street at the right. The sheet is turned with north to the right, so Marshall, Harrison, Jackson and Monroe Streets cross it from left to right and First and Second Streets run up and down. Most of the ground is laid out in lots but empty: long strips of unbuilt lots lie between Marshall and Harrison Streets and in the blocks to the left of First Street, outlined by street lines and numbered by lot. Buildings are crowded only in the blocks between First and Second Streets and along Monroe Street, where dwellings, a paper box factory, a livery stable, a hay and feed store and a bowling alley appear. Paterson Plank Road crosses the sheet as a broad diagonal street, with a varnish factory and a row of small buildings along it, and a railroad with coal pockets runs along the top. New York Avenue is lettered on a street at the left. Notes marking Volumes 3 and 4 show neighbouring sheets, and block numbers 4 to 15 and 23 to 27 are printed. A compass arrow is at the upper left.
notes: Old Paterson Plank Road is today's Paterson Avenue in Hoboken.
Most of the area west of First Street was laid out but not built in 1891.
Hoboken, 50 ft. Marshall to Monroe St, Ferry St to Second St, Paterson Plank Road (now Paterson Avenue); Jersey City side (x < 4300) masked out.

sheet-26.description: Sheet 26 of the 1891 Hoboken volume covers the western edge of the city between Second Street and Fifth Street, from the Jersey City boundary at the top to Monroe Street at the bottom. The sheet is turned on the page: the numbered streets run up and down it and north points to the right, so the named streets cross it from left to right in long horizontal rows. It is drawn at 50 feet to an inch, and street widths (50 and 65 feet), lot depths and house numbers are printed throughout. Marshall, Harrison, Jackson and Monroe Streets cross the sheet from left to right; Second, Third, Fourth and Fifth Streets run up and down. The blocks are numbered 35 to 37, 44 to 47 and 54 to 57. The top of the sheet is crossed by the railroad (N. Y. L. E. and W. R. R. and N. J. J. R. R.) in Jersey City, and a dash-dot line marked as the boundary line between Hoboken and Jersey City curves along the north edge of the built blocks, so blocks 35, 44 and 54 are cut off short against it. The area is almost unbuilt: a few small dwellings and sheds stand along Marshall Street between Third and Fourth Streets and near the Jackson Street corner at Second Street, and one building stands at the foot of block 47. The sheet is lettered Jersey City above the boundary. References Vol. 4 Sh. 30 and Vol. 4 Sh. 31 point to the Jersey City volume. A scale bar and the copyright line are printed at the lower right.
notes: Numbered streets are printed in words on this sheet; today they are 2nd to 5th Street.
Marshall Street is not used as control; only one modern Marshall Street junction exists near this sheet.
Hoboken, 50 ft. Second to Fifth St, Marshall to Monroe St, Jersey City line at top.

sheet-27.description: Sheet 27 of the 1891 Hoboken volume covers the western edge of the city between Fifth Street and Eighth Street, from the Jersey City boundary at the top to Monroe Street at the bottom. The sheet is turned on the page: the numbered streets run up and down it and north points to the right, so the named streets cross it from left to right in long horizontal rows. It is drawn at 50 feet to an inch, and street widths (50 and 65 feet), lot depths and house numbers are printed throughout. Harrison, Jackson and Monroe Streets cross the sheet from left to right, with the end of Marshall Street lettered at the upper left; Fifth, Sixth, Seventh and Eighth Streets run up and down. The blocks are numbered 64 to 66, 72 to 74 and 80 and 81. The railroad of the N. Y. L. E. and W. R. R. and N. J. J. R. R. crosses the upper part of the sheet diagonally in Jersey City, and the boundary line between Hoboken and Jersey City, drawn as a dash-dot line, cuts blocks 64, 72, 73 and 80 off along a slanting edge. Most of the lots are empty; a few buildings stand in block 74, between Sixth and Seventh Streets, near Monroe Street, and in block 81 and on the Eighth Street corner. The area above the boundary is lettered Jersey City, with references to Vol. 4 Sh. 31 and Vol. 4 Sh. 37. A scale bar, a stamp of the Princeton library and the copyright line are at the bottom.
notes: Numbered streets are printed in words on this sheet; today they are 5th to 8th Street.
The fitted scale is about 1 percent larger than the other sheets of the volume.
Hoboken, 50 ft. Fifth to Eighth St, Marshall to Monroe St, Jersey City line at top. 8th St junctions undetected.

sheet-28.description: Sheet 28 of the 1891 Hoboken volume covers the western edge of the city between Eighth Street and Eleventh Street, from the boundary with Jersey City and West Hoboken at the top to Monroe Street at the bottom. The sheet is turned on the page: the numbered streets run up and down it and north points to the right, so the named streets cross it from left to right in long horizontal rows. It is drawn at 50 feet to an inch, and street widths (50 and 65 feet), lot depths and house numbers are printed throughout. Only two rows of streets appear: Jackson Street, with the upper row of short blocks 86, 92 and part of 97 above it, and Monroe Street, below the full blocks 87, 93 and 97. Eighth, Ninth, Tenth and Eleventh Streets run up and down. The railroad of the N. Y. L. E. and W. R. R. and N. J. J. R. R. crosses the upper part of the sheet diagonally, and the boundary line between Hoboken and Jersey City, then Hoboken and West Hoboken, is drawn as a dash-dot line, cutting the upper blocks into wedges. Two oblique lines at the upper left mark a road or right-of-way crossing the railroad. Almost all lots are empty; a single small building stands in block 93. The lower half of the sheet is blank paper belonging to sheet 22, with the references Vol. 4 Sh. 37 and Vol. 8 Sh. 1. A scale bar and the copyright line are printed at the lower right.
notes: Numbered streets are printed in words (Eleventh is printed abbreviated as 'Eleventh St.'); today they are 8th to 11th Street.
Only four detected junctions and one hand-picked point control this sheet; its fitted rotation is about 1 degree less than its neighbours.
Hoboken, 50 ft. Eighth to Eleventh St, Jackson and Monroe St only; hand pick at 11th / Monroe. 5 points: low-medium confidence.
